newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraq's oil starts to flow again through Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's oil starts to flow again through Gulf.

text.p: Two huge oil tankers filled with Iraqi crude are about to move through the Gulf in Baghdad's first oil exports through the strategic waterway in six years, Gulf shipping sources said on Tuesday.

The resumption of Iraqi sales comes with an added bonus for President Saddam Hussein -- its first customers are American despite the U.S. role as leader of the allied effort that expelled Iraqi invaders from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.

The two cargoes, chartered by Texas-based Coastal Corp and trading outfit Bayoil, were expected to leave Iraq's Mina al-Bakr export terminal in the northern Gulf over the next 24 hours, shipping sources said.

"The Iraqis have been able to load the cargoes quickly...The (tanker) Star of Africa will depart tonight," one source said, referring to Coastal's chartered vessel which is expected to take approximately two million barrels of Iraqi crude to the company's refinery on the Caribbean island of Aruba.
Coastal has secured a contract to lift 60,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude under a United Nations oil-for-food deal which allows Iraq to export $2 billion of oil over six months.
Bayoil's 272,000 deadweight tonne Leonidas chartered tanker was expected to complete loading on Tuesday and depart on Wednesday as part of what trading sources said was a 30,000 bpd contract.
Iraq's first export of oil under the agreement was on Monday when Turkish refiner TUPRAS took delivery of Iraqi crude at the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.

Although the oil-for-food deal stipulates that the larger share of Iraqi oil sales will be from Turkey's Ceyhan terminal, Mina al-Bakr plays an important role in Baghdad's efforts to regain customers lost since the 1990-1991 Gulf crisis.

In particular the terminal, 12 miles (19 km) off the southern Fao Peninsula, allows the country's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) to secure customers in lucrative and import-dependent Asian markets.
Japanese energy companies have already signed contracts with SOMO to lift crude though these still await U.N. approval.

The United Nations has so far approved six crude contracts under the oil-for-food deal which Gulf traders say are Coastal, Bayoil, TUPRAS, Dutch trading firm Trafigura, Italian refiner Oil Energy and France's Elf Aquitaine.
SOMO is pursuing contract talks with at least 20 firms.
At current international oil prices Baghdad is expected to export between 500,000 and 600,000 bpd, less than one percent of total world supply.
It was exporting 2.7 million bpd on the eve of its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
